drapeaux.note: Formule de Waugh rapportée à la séance (« un nom par lequel elle sera connue des géographes… »), donnée en français ; original anglais, lettre du colonel Waugh, Journal of the Asiatic Society of Bengal, 1856. Retraduite depuis le français.

titre: Mount Everest, Named in 1856 for Lack of a Known Local Name
accroche: The world's highest summit bears the name of a man with no part in its discovery, chosen by a surveyor who said he knew of no other.
contenu_vulgarise:
Calcutta, August 1856, monthly meeting of the Asiatic Society of Bengal. Major Thuillier asks for the floor to make an announcement that, he admits, should first have gone through the Council. He reports a letter from Colonel Waugh, head of the Great Trigonometrical Survey of India: the summit the registers designate by the number XV exceeds Kangchenjunga by 846 feet. It reaches 29,002 feet, or about 8,840 meters, about a hundred miles northeast of Kathmandu.

## The Mechanism

The Survey's surveyors numbered peaks in Roman numerals: Kangchenjunga was IX, and XV had no name. Sightings were taken from the plain, more than 170 kilometers from the mountain, because Nepal was closed to foreigners. The observations date from 1849, and the calculations, carried out by the team of chief computer Radhanath Sikdar, lasted years.

Waugh states in his letter that his rule is to give every geographical object its local name. For this mountain, he could not discover any, and he will probably not know of one until Nepal can be entered. He therefore takes the privilege of naming it, in the words reported at the meeting: a name by which it will be known to geographers and become familiar to all civilized nations. It will be “Mount Everest,” in honor of his predecessor George Everest, whom he succeeded at the head of the service. The letter to Thuillier is dated March 1856, the public announcement summer.

## The Shift

Told after the fact, the christening looks like a consensual tribute to a great geodesist. The report of the following meeting shows something else. The Society's Council considers it desirable to seek the native name of the mountain, whose existence it thinks hardly in doubt, through the Nepalese government or otherwise. In the meantime, it proposes calling it by Waugh's name rather than Everest's, who, despite his merits, had had no direct connection with this discovery. A letter to that effect to Waugh is considered, then dropped after discussion: several members find it unkind to intervene.

The Council was right on the substance. The Tibetan name Qomolangma is attested in Chinese transcription in the atlas of the Kangxi Emperor in 1721, and it appears in the West in 1733 on a map by d'Anville. The Royal Geographical Society officially adopts “Mount Everest” in 1865. The name the 1856 Council asked to have sought had thus appeared in a Chinese atlas for 135 years.

repere.texte: At the August 1856 meeting of the Asiatic Society of Bengal, Major Thuillier announces a peak of 29,002 feet, 846 feet more than Kangchenjunga (28,156 feet). Colonel Waugh says he has discovered no local name for this peak.
repere.source: Journal of the Asiatic Society of Bengal, No. 5, 1856, pp. 437-439 (Proceedings of the Asiatic Society)

carte.punch: In 1856, the world's highest summit gets a name because no other could be found.
carte.idee: Waugh announces a peak of 29,002 feet and says he has discovered no local name. He calls it Everest, after his predecessor. The Asiatic Society of Bengal asks that the native name be sought, and proposes writing Waugh rather than Everest.

quiz.question: Why does the summit receive the name Everest in 1856?
choix: George Everest had measured it in 1849 and the Survey wanted to reward him
The Council of the Asiatic Society had voted for this name unanimously before the announcement
Waugh says he found no local name and chooses that of his predecessor
The Nepalese government had asked for a British name for the mountain
quiz.explication: Waugh writes that he could not discover any local name, Nepal being closed to foreigners, and reserves the privilege of naming the peak. Everest had had no direct connection with this discovery. The Council of the Asiatic Society, far from voting for this name, proposed writing Waugh and seeking the native name.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why were the sightings of peak XV taken from more than 170 kilometers away?
choix: Because the instruments of the time could not measure from closer
Because Nepal was closed to foreigners
Because the summit was inaccessible in every season
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text specifies that sightings were taken from the plain, more than 170 kilometers away, because Nepal was closed to foreigners, not because of the instruments, the accessibility of the summit, or avalanche risk.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What did the Council of the Asiatic Society of Bengal propose at the meeting following Waugh's announcement?
choix: To seek the native name and call the mountain by Waugh's name rather than Everest's
To confirm the choice of the name Everest unanimously
To also rename Kangchenjunga in honor of Radhanath Sikdar
To wait for Nepal to open before publishing the summit's height
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The Council judges that the native name probably exists, proposes seeking it and calling the mountain by Waugh's name, because Everest had had no direct connection with this discovery, contrary to a unanimous vote, a tribute to Sikdar, or a postponement.
